title: The Duel of Equal Champions
story:
On the open ground outside Girivraja, two men faced each other with maces in their hands, and the dust between them might as well have been a battlefield. Jarasandha, the king of Magadha, had ruled that city for years on a strength no one had ever matched. Bhima, the second of the five Pandava brothers, had come there with his brother Arjuna and their cousin Krishna, disguised, to free the kings Jarasandha held prisoner; and when Krishna threw off the disguise and demanded battle, Jarasandha had looked the three of them over and chosen Bhima as his opponent. It was the choice of a man who wants to break the strongest one first.

Now they stood facing each other, and for a long moment neither moved. Then both raised their great maces and closed in. The first blows would have finished lesser men: the clubs came down with the full weight of both arms behind them, and the sound of their meeting rolled across the field like the clash of a thunderbolt, sharp and dry.

The two champions began to circle, moving in wide, intricate patterns, turning now left, now right, like wrestlers who had spent a lifetime reading each other's feet. Each watched for the instant the rhythm would break — a shoulder dipping too far, a heel sliding in the dust. Neither found it. Every step was answered, every rush met, every opening closed the moment it appeared.

Then the maces began to give way. Blow after blow, the great clubs of both men shattered under the force of the exchange, splintering like brittle twigs, until each champion was left holding a ruined staff.

Anger did the rest. Dropping what was left of their weapons, the two men fell on each other with their bare hands, striking with fists hard as iron. The blows landed on shoulders and chests and sides, and the sound of fist on flesh was harsh and heavy across the field. Neither man gave ground. Bhima's strength had never met its match; Jarasandha's had never met its equal. They were matched in skill, matched in strength, matched in the fire that drives a fighter, and every advantage one of them seized, the other answered before it could be pressed.

By the time the light began to slant over the city walls, the duel was still not decided. Both champions stood breathing hard, bruised and battered, their ruined maces lying in the dust where they had dropped them. Neither had fallen, and neither would fall.

And so the great duel of the two champions remained unfinished — not for lack of fury, but because fury alone could not break the balance between them. Bhima looked across at his enemy and saw something like himself: the same pride, the same iron fists, the same refusal to fall. The fight could have gone on until the next dawn, and the one after that, and still neither man would have yielded.

Only one man on that field knew the duel could not end this way. Krishna had not crossed the country to watch two equal champions wear each other down; he had come to end a threat. He watched in silence, waiting for the moment that would end it.
reflection: The duel is left unfinished not because either man weakens but because they are exactly matched; Bhima's strength meets a strength like his own, and endurance alone cannot break the deadlock. Krishna watches, knowing that a fight this even can never be won by fighting.
content_note: A sustained mace and fist duel; intense but described without graphic detail.
next_story_tease: But Krishna had not come to Girivraja to watch a duel that could never end; he knew the one secret that could finish it.
hero_scene: Bhima and Jarasandha circling each other on the open ground outside Girivraja, their great maces raised for the next blow, splintered fragments of their shattered clubs scattered in the dust between them.
